newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Workers high, immigrants low among Aussie patriots.
newsitem.headline: Workers high, immigrants low among Aussie patriots.

text.p: Australian academics in search of the nation's patriotic heart have found that it beats strongly among poor "battlers" but faintly in immigrants.
Their study, published on Monday, suggests Australia's strongest patriots may live in the kind of working-class constituency represented by race-row politician Pauline Hanson.
Its weakest patriots include citizens who migrated to Australia and the nation's educated elite, according to the study, "Pride and Commitment: Patriotism in Australia".

"Migrants...turned up as pretty unpatriotic and I was surprised and a little bit sad because it's not what I thought we would find," said sociologist Dr Katharine Betts, one of the study's co-authors.
But Betts, of Swinburne University, and colleague Virginia Rapson of Monash University, were not surprised Australia's less educated, jobless and retired masses emerged as the strongest patriots.
"That's what we thought we would find and that's what we did find," Betts told Reuters in Melbourne.
The two researchers examined data from a 1996 survey of about 1,800 voters taken after the March general election, which handed a landslide victory to the major conservative parties.
The survey asked people to express their pride in Australia, its various achievements and history, and if they agreed they would "rather be a citizen of Australia than any other country".

In response to the second question, 75 percent of Australian-born citizens strongly agreed whereas only 37 percent of overseas-born citizens strongly agreed. Of the foreign-born, immigrants from English-speaking countries were least patriotic.
When education levels were looked at, the study showed 71 percent of those who did not go beyond high school strongly agreed compared with 58 percent for university graduates.
The study does not refer directly to Hanson, a fish and chip shop owner turned legislator whose call for a freeze on immigration has struck a chord with voters nation-wide.
But Betts said Hanson's supporters, if not Hanson herself, were likely to be strong patriots, clinging to patriotic symbols during times of major social and economic change.

"You could say she came from running a little shop...if she was not economically threatened herself, she certainly was dealing with people who were and that's where we would expect to find our strongest patriots," Betts said.

"There has been a fair bit the battlers have had to cope with. This original theory of people feeling under threat, wanting to cling to national symbols and national idea...I think it does help explain the support that Hanson has received," she added.
